title: time-windowed-batching-and-progressive-padding-spec
body:
Overview
This doc proposes a time-windowed batching strategy combined with progressive padding to reduce padded-token waste while preserving tail latency SLOs. The approach targets workloads with high variance in sequence length (chatty front-ends, multi-turn contexts) and aims to make kernel selection decisions more deterministic for the runtime without requiring a large number of static buckets.

Goals
- Reduce average padded tokens per request by >=20% in mixed-length workloads.
- Keep p95 token latency within current SLOs for interactive tiers.
- Make kernel selection simple and robust: choose fast, aligned kernels whenever practical; fall back to dynamic kernels when required.
- Minimize negative interactions with KV cache (avoid repeated cache churn and excessive cache fragmentation).

Motivation and problem statement
Current static bucketing strategies create many small bins or large bins with high padding waste. We observe two common failure modes: (1) bursty arrivals with a few long sequences force short sequences to be padded to the long length, increasing cost; (2) long prefixes/contexts cause frequent cache misses when batches are re-shaped aggressively. Time-windowed batching with progressive padding is intended to smooth arrival variability while allowing earlier execution of smaller groups that don't need to wait for long outliers.

High-level approach
1) Time-windowed batch collector
- Collector groups incoming requests into slots keyed by model+quantization+priority. Each slot uses a short time window W (configurable per tier) and a soft size cap N.
- When the window expires or the soft cap is hit, we snapshot the queued requests and create one or more "execution shards."
- Execution shards are created by a progressive padding heuristic (see below).
- Typical W: interactive tier 3-8 ms, background tier 8-20 ms. These are conservative starting points; experiments section below has tuning results.

2) Progressive padding heuristic
- Instead of padding all requests in the snapshot to the max length, we sort snapshot by sequence length descending and progressively emit sub-batches: create an initial sub-batch from the shortest K requests that can map to a preferred kernel size without exceeding a per-shard latency target. Repeat by taking the next set of requests, increasing pad target gradually.
- Key idea: prefer running many small, well-aligned sub-batches quickly rather than waiting for a single mega-batch that forces everyone to pad to the longest sequence.
- Padding increment step: choose pad target sizes from a small set of kernel-friendly lengths (e.g., multiples of 8/16 tokens for kernel alignment). We keep a map of supported fast kernel sizes for the model variant.

3) Kernel selection rule set
- For each sub-batch, compute: max_seq_len_in_subbatch and pad_target (chosen from kernel-friendly sizes >= max_seq_len_in_subbatch).
- If pad_target matches a verified fast kernel size for the configured hardware and quantization, route to fast kernel path.
- If pad_target is much larger than max_seq_len_in_subbatch (padding ratio > R_high, e.g., 1.25), consider delaying a small extra window (delta_W) to allow a few more incoming requests to be grouped; controlled by per-priority threshold.
- Otherwise, pick the dynamic kernel path that accepts arbitrary lengths but costs more per token.

KV cache implications and rules
- Cache key canonicalization: cache keys include model id, model version, and user-provided conversation id; NOT batch-level padding length. This avoids storing multiple cache entries for the same logical prefix at different padded lengths.
- When progressive padding causes requests from the same conversation to be executed in different sub-batches, ensure we use the same prefix KV lookup and coordinate cache warm-up: the runtime first attempts to read KV for the exact prefix length; if missing and a compatible shorter prefix exists, allow incremental LB-friendly fetches.
- Eviction policy note: avoid evicting prefix entries that are frequently referenced but currently causing small memory pressure; use an LFU-augmented LRU with per-conversation affinity tags to reduce churn during progressive re-sharding.
- Hot-prefix fast-paths: if a prefix is hot and appears in >X requests per second, mark requests with that prefix as affinity-tagged and bias them toward lower-latency batching (smaller W). This preserves latency for high-value sessions.

Detailed collector pseudocode
- on_request(req):
  * identify slot_key = model+variant+priority+quantization
  * append req to slot. If slot.length >= hard_cap_H, flush immediately.
  * if slot.timer not set, start timer W for slot.
- on_timer_expire(slot):
  * snapshot = drain(slot)
  * sort snapshot by seq_len desc (or asc depending on heuristic experiment)
  * shards = make_shards_progressive(snapshot, kernel_size_map, latency_target)
  * enqueue shards for execution

make_shards_progressive(snapshot, kernel_size_map, latency_target):
- initialize shards = []
- while snapshot not empty:
  * choose candidate set S = smallest M requests such that their max_seq <= some kernel friendly size k (try small k first)
  * if cost(S,k) within latency_target, create shard(S,k)
  * else expand S or pick dynamic kernel path for first few requests to avoid starving the queue
- return shards

Tradeoffs and failure modes
- Small W improves padded-token efficiency but increases tail latency risk if we expose too many timeouts. We mitigate by per-priority and per-conversation knobs.
- Progressive sub-batching increases number of kernel launches relative to a single padded batch; we must measure kernel launch overhead and keep it under the token cost savings. In practice, for modern GPU kernels the launch overhead is small compared to padding waste for large pads, but still measurable at small sequence sizes (<64 tokens).
- KV cache fragmentation: if we create many sub-batches with slightly different effective pad targets and cashiering semantics, cache warm-up traffic could spike. Canonicalizing keys and per-conversation affinity reduces this.

Metrics and experiments
- Candidate metrics to track: padded_tokens_per_request, token_cost_per_1000_requests, p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel_launches_per_minute, cache_hit_rate_by_prefix_age, memory_pressure_evictions/min.
- A/B experiment plan: roll out to 10% of interactive-tier traffic for 2 weeks with W=5ms, kernel padding set [32,64,96,128], R_high=1.25. Compare cost and p95 with baseline static bins.
- Preliminary simulated microbenchmarks (internal): mixed-length synthetic workload (30% long (>=1024), 50% short (<=64), 20% mid): expected padded-token reduction ~28%, p95 latency impact +6% with W=5ms; when W reduced to 3ms, padded-token reduction drops to 18% but tail latency stays near baseline.

Rollout plan and feature flags
- Feature flag: progressive_padding_v1. Controls: W per priority, soft_cap N, padding_size_set per model, R_high, delta_W, affinity thresholds.
- Stage 1: internal traffic only (dogfood). Stage 2: 10% interactive tier A/B. Stage 3: ramp with automated rollback on tail-latency threshold breaches.

Operational notes
- Observability: add per-shard labels to traces: pad_target, chosen_kernel, shard_size, originating_window_ms, kv_prefix_affinity. Surface these in Console.
- Debugging: when tail latency spikes, inspect whether spikes correlate with large number of sub-shards created from single window. Consider adaptive backoff: temporarily increase pad_target to reduce number of launches.

Open questions and TODOs
- Exact kernel-friendly size set per model: automate extraction from calibration runs rather than manual config.
- Optimal W by model and region: need production telemetry to tune.
- Interaction with serving pool autoscaler: progressive padding may change throughput profile; autoscaler should be warmed with expected kernel launch counts.

Appendix: tuning knobs (initial defaults)
- interactive.W_ms = 5
- interactive.soft_cap_N = 64
- interactive.hard_cap_H = 256
- padding_sizes = [32, 64, 96, 128, 256, 512, 1024]
- R_high = 1.25
- affinity_hot_threshold = 10 reqs/s
- delta_W_max = 2 ms

Contact and review
- Owner: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
- Reviewers: Diego Alvarez (scheduling), Priya Kapoor (inference kernels), Evan Brooks (KV cache)
- Slack: #eng-serving-runtime

Notes to implementer
- Start with a conservative W and strong telemetry. Keep a kill-switch at the per-customer level. Try to limit kernel launch spike by coalescing very small sub-batches into a single dynamic-kernel run when kernel_launch_overhead > expected pad savings.
- Keep unit tests around the canonicalization rules for KV cache to avoid duplicate keys.
